title: Particle Model, Gases & Temperature
description: States of matter, the kinetic particle model, Brownian motion, absolute temperature, gas pressure and Boyle's law for IGCSE Physics 0625.

notes.heading: States of Matter and the Particle Model
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The **kinetic particle model** pictures all matter as tiny particles in motion. The three states of matter differ in the arrangement and movement of their particles.

🔑 How it works
• **Solid** — particles touch in a fixed, regular arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions. A solid keeps its own shape and volume.
• **Liquid** — particles touch but are arranged irregularly and slide past one another. A liquid keeps its volume but flows to fit its container.
• **Gas** — particles are far apart and move rapidly in random directions. A gas expands to fill its container and can be compressed.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Density falls from solid to liquid to gas mainly because the **spacing** of the particles increases.
• The particles themselves do not change when the state changes — only their arrangement and motion.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Drawing liquid particles widely separated. Liquid particles are as close together as in the solid — they are just disordered and free to move past each other.

notes.heading: Explaining Properties with Particles
notes.body:
🔑 How it works
The properties of each state follow from the **forces** between particles, their **distances** apart and their **motion** (the Supplement wording of the syllabus):
• Solids: strong forces hold particles in fixed positions → fixed shape, cannot be compressed, high density.
• Liquids: forces are still strong enough to keep particles close, but weak enough to let them move → flows, fixed volume, almost incompressible.
• Gases: negligible forces between fast-moving, widely spaced particles → expands without limit, easily compressed, low density.

💡 Worked Example
Why can a gas be compressed when a solid cannot? A gas is mostly empty space between particles, so the particles can be pushed closer together; solid particles are already touching.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• In the exam, explain with forces, distances AND motion of the particles — all three score marks.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying gas particles 'expand' when heated. The particles stay the same size; they move faster and spread further apart.

notes.heading: Brownian Motion — Evidence for the Model
notes.body:
📌 Definition
**Brownian motion** is the continuous, random, jerky movement of microscopic particles suspended in a fluid.

🔑 The smoke-cell experiment
Smoke is trapped in a small glass cell, brightly lit from the side and viewed through a microscope. The smoke specks appear as bright points that dart about randomly, never settling into a steady path.

🔑 Explanation
Each visible speck is bombarded **unevenly** by vast numbers of fast-moving, invisible air molecules; at any instant more molecules strike one side than the other, so the speck lurches. The observed motion of the specks is evidence for the unseen motion of the molecules.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Brownian motion is evidence for the kinetic particle model: matter is made of tiny particles in continuous random motion.
• The specks do not move because they are 'alive' or because of the light.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Claiming you see the air molecules. You see the **smoke particles**; the air molecules are far too small to see.

notes.heading: Temperature, Absolute Zero and the Kelvin Scale
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles. The **kelvin** (K) is the SI unit of temperature. **Absolute zero**, $0\text{ K} = -273^{\circ}\text{C}$, is the temperature at which the particles have minimum possible kinetic energy.

🔑 How it works
To convert between the scales, add 273: $T(\text{K}) = \theta(^{\circ}\text{C}) + 273$.
• $0^{\circ}\text{C} = 273\text{ K}$ and $100^{\circ}\text{C} = 373\text{ K}$.
• A temperature **change** of $1^{\circ}\text{C}$ is exactly the same as a change of $1\text{ K}$.

💡 Worked Example
Room temperature, $20^{\circ}\text{C}$, is $20 + 273 = 293\text{ K}$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, so kelvin temperatures are proportional to the particles' average kinetic energy.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing a kelvin temperature with a degree sign — it is $300\text{ K}$, never $300^{\circ}\text{K}$.

notes.heading: Gas Pressure and the Particle Model
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A gas exerts pressure because its particles **collide with the walls** of the container. Each collision exerts a small force on the wall; billions of collisions per second spread over the wall's area give a steady pressure.

🔑 How it works (Core, qualitative)
• **Heat the gas at constant volume** — the particles move faster, so they hit the walls harder and more often → pressure increases.
• **Squeeze the gas at constant temperature** — the same particles now have less space, so they hit the walls more often → pressure increases.

💡 Worked Example
An aerosol can warns 'keep away from heat': the volume is fixed, so heating raises the pressure, and the can may burst.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always explain a pressure change in terms of the **rate and force of collisions** — those are the mark-scheme words.

⚠️ Common Mistake
'The pressure rises because the particles expand.' Particles do not expand; they collide harder and more frequently.

notes.heading: Boyle's Law — pV = constant (Supplement)
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Supplement content. For a **fixed mass of gas at constant temperature**, pressure is inversely proportional to volume:

$$pV = \text{constant} \qquad p_1V_1 = p_2V_2$$

💡 Worked Example
$200\text{ cm}^3$ of gas at $100\text{ kPa}$ is compressed slowly to $50\text{ cm}^3$ at constant temperature:

$$p_2 = \dfrac{p_1V_1}{V_2} = \dfrac{100 \times 200}{50} = 400\text{ kPa}$$

🔑 The two graphs
• $p$ against $V$: a smooth curve that falls steeply and then flattens — the signature of an inverse relationship.
• $p$ against $1/V$: a **straight line through the origin**, showing $p \propto \dfrac{1}{V}$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The law applies only if the mass and the temperature of the gas are fixed — quote that condition in the exam.
• Halving the volume doubles the pressure; tripling the volume divides the pressure by three.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using Boyle's law while the gas is being heated. If the temperature changes, $pV$ is not constant.

illustration.alt: Two graphs for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature: pressure against volume forms a falling curve, and pressure against 1 over volume forms a straight line through the origin.
illustration.caption: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pV is constant — an inverse curve against V, a straight line through the origin against 1/V.

notes.heading: Explaining Pressure Changes with Particles (Supplement)
notes.body:
🔑 How it works
Supplement content. Every pressure change can be explained by the **rate** and **force** of particle collisions with the walls:
• **Smaller volume, same temperature** — the particles move at the same average speed but have less far to travel between wall collisions, so collisions are more **frequent** → higher pressure.
• **Higher temperature, same volume** — the particles move faster, so collisions are more frequent **and** each collision exerts a greater force → higher pressure.
• **Bigger volume, same temperature** — collisions become less frequent → lower pressure.

💡 Worked Example
A sealed syringe of air is pushed in slowly so the temperature stays constant. The same number of particles is confined to a smaller volume; each area of wall is struck more times per second, so the pressure rises until it balances your thumb.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• 'Particles hit the walls more often' scores the mark for a volume change; 'harder and more often' for a temperature change.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying heating 'makes more particles'. The number of particles in a sealed container is fixed.

flashcards.example: Ice keeps its own shape until it melts.

flashcards.definition: Particles touch but are disordered and slide past one another; a liquid keeps its volume but flows to fit its container.
flashcards.example: Water poured from a jug takes the shape of the glass.

flashcards.definition: Particles are far apart and move rapidly at random; a gas fills its container and can be compressed.
flashcards.example: Air in a syringe can be squeezed to a smaller volume.

flashcards.definition: All matter is made of tiny particles in continuous motion; the states differ in the arrangement, spacing and motion of the particles.
flashcards.example: Solids, liquids and gases of the same substance contain identical particles.

flashcards.definition: The continuous, random, jerky motion of microscopic particles suspended in a fluid; evidence for the kinetic particle model.
flashcards.example: Pollen grains dancing in a drop of water under a microscope.

flashcards.definition: Lit smoke in a glass cell viewed under a microscope: bright specks dart randomly because invisible air molecules bombard them unevenly.
flashcards.example: The specks lurch because more molecules strike one side than the other at any instant.

flashcards.definition: 0 K = −273 °C; the temperature at which particles have the minimum possible kinetic energy.
flashcards.example: An ideal gas would exert zero pressure at absolute zero — no particle motion, no wall collisions.

Caused by gas particles colliding with the container walls; the pressure is the combined effect of billions of collisions per second.
flashcards.example: A balloon stays inflated because air particles keep striking its inner surface.

flashcards.example: This is why a sealed aerosol can may burst on a hot windowsill.

choices: are far apart and move randomly
vibrate about fixed positions in a regular arrangement
questions.explanation: Solid particles touch in a fixed, regular arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions — that is why a solid keeps its own shape. They are never completely still.

questions.stem: Brownian motion is the observation that...
choices: tiny particles suspended in a fluid move continuously and randomly
gases always expand when they are heated
questions.explanation: Brownian motion is the random jerky movement of suspended microscopic particles, caused by uneven bombardment from invisible molecules — evidence for the kinetic particle model.
$T(\text{K}) = \theta(^{\circ}\text{C}) + 273 = 27 + 273 = 300\text{ K}$. The 246 K option subtracts instead of adding.

choices: −273 °C (0 K), where particles have minimum possible kinetic energy
−100 °C, the coldest natural temperature on Earth
the temperature at which all gases liquefy
questions.explanation: Absolute zero is $-273^{\circ}\text{C} = 0\text{ K}$, the lower limit of temperature, where particle kinetic energy is at its minimum.

questions.stem: A gas exerts pressure on its container because...
choices: its particles collide with the walls
questions.explanation: Pressure is the combined effect of billions of particle collisions with the walls every second — each collision exerts a small force on the wall.
$\theta = 373 - 273 = 100^{\circ}\text{C}$ — the boiling point of water. The 646 °C option adds 273 instead of subtracting.

questions.stem: A sealed rigid container of gas is heated. The pressure rises because the particles...
choices: expand and push the walls harder
move faster, so they hit the walls harder and more frequently
questions.explanation: Heating raises the particles' kinetic energy: collisions with the walls become more frequent and each collision exerts a greater force, so pressure rises. Particles do not expand, multiply or gain mass.

questions.stem: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, a graph of pressure against 1/volume is...
choices: a curve that bends away from the origin
a straight line through the origin
a straight line that misses the origin
questions.explanation: Boyle's law gives $p \propto \dfrac{1}{V}$, so $p$ against $1/V$ is a straight line through the origin. It is $p$ against $V$ that is a curve.

questions.stem: A gas occupies 200 cm³ at a pressure of 100 kPa. It is compressed slowly, so the temperature stays constant, to 50 cm³. What is the new pressure?
questions.explanation: Boyle's law: $p_2 = \dfrac{p_1V_1}{V_2} = \dfrac{100 \times 200}{50} = 400\text{ kPa}$. The volume is divided by 4, so the pressure is multiplied by 4.

questions.stem: A temperature rise of 10 °C is the same as a rise of...
questions.explanation: The kelvin and Celsius scales have identical step sizes: a **change** of $10^{\circ}\text{C}$ is a change of $10\text{ K}$. The 283 K option adds 273, which only applies when converting an actual temperature, not a change.

questions.stem: A gas at a pressure of 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa occupies 400 cm³. At constant temperature it is compressed to 250 cm³. What is the new pressure?
questions.explanation: $p_1V_1 = p_2V_2$ gives $p_2 = \dfrac{1.5 \times 10^5 \times 400}{250} = 2.4 \times 10^{5}\text{ Pa}$. The $6.0 \times 10^{5}\text{ Pa}$ option multiplies the pressures instead of dividing by the volume ratio.

questions.stem: A fixed mass of gas at constant temperature has a pressure of 120 kPa and a volume of 300 cm³. What is its volume when the pressure falls to 90 kPa?
questions.explanation: $V_2 = \dfrac{p_1V_1}{p_2} = \dfrac{120 \times 300}{90} = 400\text{ cm}^3$. The pressure has fallen, so the volume must have risen — 225 cm³ goes the wrong way.

questions.stem: Using the particle model, why does the pressure of a gas fall when its container expands at constant temperature?
choices: the particles travel further between wall collisions, so they strike the walls less frequently
the particles slow down because the container is bigger
the particles get smaller as they spread out
gravity acts on fewer of the particles
questions.explanation: At constant temperature the particles keep the same average speed, but in a larger volume each particle hits the walls less often, so the collision rate — and hence the pressure — falls. Particle size and speed are unchanged.

questions.stem: A p–V graph for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature passes through V = 2 m³, p = 100 kPa. Which other point lies on the same curve?
questions.explanation: Every point on the curve has $pV = 100 \times 2 = 200$. Only $V = 8\text{ m}^3$, $p = 25\text{ kPa}$ gives $8 \times 25 = 200$; the other pairings give 400 or 100.

questions.stem: In the smoke-cell experiment, the bright specks seen through the microscope jerk about randomly because...
choices: invisible air molecules bombard the smoke particles unevenly
the light shining on them pushes them around
the cell is heated from below
questions.explanation: At any instant more fast-moving air molecules strike one side of a speck than the other, so the speck lurches. This uneven bombardment by invisible molecules is the evidence for the kinetic particle model.
